full_text: This perspective synthesizes published evidence on Ebola vaccination and outbreak preparedness in Africa. Successful vaccination against Zaire ebolavirus has strengthened vaccine-based outbreak control but may also create a preparedness risk when public expectations exceed species-specific vaccine availability. We propose the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy as linked, hypothesis-generating constructs, supported by a Preparedness Trust Contract for practical implementation. The framework draws on expectation-disconfirmation and crisis and emergency risk communication theories and distinguishes established evidence from interpretation and testable hypotheses. Recent Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus outbreaks illustrate the relevance of this gap because licensed vaccines remain species-specific. Evidence is concentrated in Uganda, making broader East African application a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. If validated, the framework could strengthen risk communication, community trust and regional health-security planning. DiscussionWe do not intend the vaccination paradox to weaken the case for Ebola vaccines; if anything, we read it as strengthening that case, since vaccines remain among the most important tools in Ebola preparedness. Our point is narrower: vaccine success may change the social environment in which outbreaks occur. Before Ebola vaccines were widely known, communities often had to be persuaded that vaccination was possible; we hypothesize that, in parts of East and Central Africa, communities may now need to understand why vaccination is not always immediately available. If this hypothesis holds, it would represent a different communication challenge requiring different preparedness tools. The Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy, together with the Preparedness Trust Contract as a subordinate governance mechanism, offer a proposed conceptual vocabulary for this problem, shifting the discussion from a narrow focus on vaccine availability toward a broader view of vaccine governance that includes science, regulation, logistics, community trust and public expectation.As Figure 1 makes explicit, we do not claim that an expectation gap necessarily causes confusion, mistrust or reduced compliance. These outcomes plausibly depend on moderating factors such as prior outbreak experience, communication quality, media exposure, perceived equity of access and pre-existing political trust, none of which this framework has directly measured. We present the pathway from vaccine success to expectation-related mistrust as a testable hypothesis rather than a demonstrated mechanism, and we encourage future empirical work, including the community perception assessments recommended above, to test each link in this pathway rather than assuming it.East Africa, and increasingly Central Africa, are well placed to lead this research agenda. The region has direct experience with multiple ebolavirus species, cross-border outbreak risk, healthcare-worker vulnerability and community engagement challenges, alongside growing research infrastructure and experience with vaccine trials (12). We propose that the next priority is to test, empirically, whether the constructs proposed here rather than assuming their existence can be measured and used to align vaccine science with honest, anticipatory and culturally grounded communication. ConclusionEbola vaccination has become a defining, well-documented success of modern outbreak preparedness. We propose, as a hypothesis for future testing, that this success may also create new vulnerabilities. In Uganda, and potentially more broadly in East and Central Africa, communities may increasingly expect vaccines to be part of Ebola outbreak response, while vaccine availability remains species-specific and uneven across Zaire ebolavirus, Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus. This Perspective introduces the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy as hypothesis-generating constructs, and the Preparedness Trust Contract as a subordinate governance mechanism, for an emerging challenge in Ebola preparedness that has not, to our knowledge, been previously conceptualized in this way. We propose that future preparedness research test whether expectations require management alongside vaccine stocks, and whether species-specific vaccine literacy and transparent communication can prevent vaccine success from unintentionally producing disappointment during outbreaks where licensed vaccines remain unavailable. We suggest that the next phase of Ebola vaccine preparedness research in East and Central Africa should test, empirically, whether combining better vaccines with deliberate expectation governance improves community trust when the next outbreak, of whichever ebolavirus species, arrives. IntroductionEbola control has changed profoundly in the past decade. During the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic, vaccines were still largely experimental. The Ebola Ça Suffit! Ring vaccination trial later demonstrated the efficacy and effectiveness of rVSV-ZEBOV against Zaire ebolavirus disease, a landmark result in modern outbreak response (1, 21). Since then, vaccination has become part of how governments, health workers, international partners and communities imagine Ebola preparedness. This success is well documented for disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus specifically. Two vaccines are approved for this indication: the single-dose rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine and the two-dose Ad26. ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo regimen (2, 3). These products do not automatically extend to disease caused by Sudan virus or Bundibugyo virus (3, 4).That distinction matters in East and Central Africa, where Uganda has experienced Sudan virus disease and Bundibugyo virus disease, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo has repeatedly faced outbreaks of Zaire ebolavirus disease and, most recently, a large cross-border Bundibugyo virus disease emergency that began in May 2026 and led the World Health Organization Director-General to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (4, 5). We use “Ebola virus disease” specifically for disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus, “Sudan virus disease” and “Bundibugyo virus disease” for disease caused by those respective species, and “ebolavirus disease” or “Ebola disease” as the broader umbrella term covering any recognized ebolavirus species, following current WHO usage (3).Whether members of the public distinguish between ebolavirus species, and whether successful vaccination against one species generates expectations of availability against others, are empirical questions that, to our knowledge, have not yet been directly studied in East or Central Africa. We treat both as working hypotheses rather than established findings. If they hold, public health authorities responding to an outbreak caused by a species for which no licensed vaccine exists would face a difficult communication problem: explaining why a vaccine exists for one form of Ebola disease but not another, while maintaining trust during an active emergency. Preliminary, not-yet-peer-reviewed evidence from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease emergency offers some support for this concern: an analysis of public commentary on video-sharing platforms during the outbreak found that discourse was substantially shaped by institutional mistrust, misinformation and comparisons with unrelated past health emergencies, alongside expressions of trust (6). This is consistent with, but does not directly confirm, an expectation-related mistrust pathway of the kind this Perspective proposes.This Perspective proposes that East Africa’s experience with Ebola vaccine preparedness may be creating a new public health challenge, which we term the vaccination paradox: preparedness success may increase confidence, and confidence may in turn generate expectation. Where expectations exceed what vaccine science can immediately deliver, outbreak response could face avoidable mistrust although the existence and magnitude of this effect have not yet been measured. Based on a non-systematic review of the peer-reviewed and gray literature described below, we are not aware of prior work that conceptualizes this dynamic as a distinct preparedness risk in East or Central African Ebola control; we offer this as our reading of the literature rather than as a systematic bibliometric claim. We therefore introduce a hypothesis-generating framework linking vaccine science, community expectation, risk communication and regional outbreak governance, grounded explicitly in expectation-disconfirmation theory (7) and crisis and emergency risk communication theory (8).Distinguishing evidence, interpretation and hypothesisThroughout this Perspective we distinguish three categories of claim. First, established findings: facts documented in the cited primary literature, such as the existence of licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccines or the case counts of specific outbreaks. Second, interpretations: our reading of what those findings plausibly imply, stated explicitly as interpretation. Third, hypotheses: constructs and causal pathways that this Perspective proposes but that have not been directly tested, including the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation, and the proposed pathway from vaccine success to expectation-related mistrust. We flag hypotheses explicitly in the text, and Table 1 and Figure 1 mark the evidentiary status of each element of the framework. Recent Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus outbreaks illustrate the relevance of this gap because licensed vaccines remain species-specific. Evidence is concentrated in Uganda, making broader East African application a hypothesis requiring empirical testing. If validated, the framework could strengthen risk communication, community trust and regional health-security planning.
full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionWe do not intend the vaccination paradox to weaken the case for Ebola vaccines; if anything, we read it as strengthening that case, since vaccines remain among the most important tools in Ebola preparedness. Our point is narrower: vaccine success may change the social environment in which outbreaks occur. Before Ebola vaccines were widely known, communities often had to be persuaded that vaccination was possible; we hypothesize that, in parts of East and Central Africa, communities may now need to understand why vaccination is not always immediately available. If this hypothesis holds, it would represent a different communication challenge requiring different preparedness tools. The Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy, together with the Preparedness Trust Contract as a subordinate governance mechanism, offer a proposed conceptual vocabulary for this problem, shifting the discussion from a narrow focus on vaccine availability toward a broader view of vaccine governance that includes science, regulation, logistics, community trust and public expectation.As Figure 1 makes explicit, we do not claim that an expectation gap necessarily causes confusion, mistrust or reduced compliance. These outcomes plausibly depend on moderating factors such as prior outbreak experience, communication quality, media exposure, perceived equity of access and pre-existing political trust, none of which this framework has directly measured. We present the pathway from vaccine success to expectation-related mistrust as a testable hypothesis rather than a demonstrated mechanism, and we encourage future empirical work, including the community perception assessments recommended above, to test each link in this pathway rather than assuming it.East Africa, and increasingly Central Africa, are well placed to lead this research agenda. The region has direct experience with multiple ebolavirus species, cross-border outbreak risk, healthcare-worker vulnerability and community engagement challenges, alongside growing research infrastructure and experience with vaccine trials (12). We propose that the next priority is to test, empirically, whether the constructs proposed here rather than assuming their existence can be measured and used to align vaccine science with honest, anticipatory and culturally grounded communication.
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionEbola vaccination has become a defining, well-documented success of modern outbreak preparedness. We propose, as a hypothesis for future testing, that this success may also create new vulnerabilities. In Uganda, and potentially more broadly in East and Central Africa, communities may increasingly expect vaccines to be part of Ebola outbreak response, while vaccine availability remains species-specific and uneven across Zaire ebolavirus, Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus. This Perspective introduces the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation and Species-Specific Vaccine Literacy as hypothesis-generating constructs, and the Preparedness Trust Contract as a subordinate governance mechanism, for an emerging challenge in Ebola preparedness that has not, to our knowledge, been previously conceptualized in this way. We propose that future preparedness research test whether expectations require management alongside vaccine stocks, and whether species-specific vaccine literacy and transparent communication can prevent vaccine success from unintentionally producing disappointment during outbreaks where licensed vaccines remain unavailable. We suggest that the next phase of Ebola vaccine preparedness research in East and Central Africa should test, empirically, whether combining better vaccines with deliberate expectation governance improves community trust when the next outbreak, of whichever ebolavirus species, arrives.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionEbola control has changed profoundly in the past decade. During the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic, vaccines were still largely experimental. The Ebola Ça Suffit! Ring vaccination trial later demonstrated the efficacy and effectiveness of rVSV-ZEBOV against Zaire ebolavirus disease, a landmark result in modern outbreak response (1, 21). Since then, vaccination has become part of how governments, health workers, international partners and communities imagine Ebola preparedness. This success is well documented for disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus specifically. Two vaccines are approved for this indication: the single-dose rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine and the two-dose Ad26. ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo regimen (2, 3). These products do not automatically extend to disease caused by Sudan virus or Bundibugyo virus (3, 4).That distinction matters in East and Central Africa, where Uganda has experienced Sudan virus disease and Bundibugyo virus disease, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo has repeatedly faced outbreaks of Zaire ebolavirus disease and, most recently, a large cross-border Bundibugyo virus disease emergency that began in May 2026 and led the World Health Organization Director-General to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (4, 5). We use “Ebola virus disease” specifically for disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus, “Sudan virus disease” and “Bundibugyo virus disease” for disease caused by those respective species, and “ebolavirus disease” or “Ebola disease” as the broader umbrella term covering any recognized ebolavirus species, following current WHO usage (3).Whether members of the public distinguish between ebolavirus species, and whether successful vaccination against one species generates expectations of availability against others, are empirical questions that, to our knowledge, have not yet been directly studied in East or Central Africa. We treat both as working hypotheses rather than established findings. If they hold, public health authorities responding to an outbreak caused by a species for which no licensed vaccine exists would face a difficult communication problem: explaining why a vaccine exists for one form of Ebola disease but not another, while maintaining trust during an active emergency. Preliminary, not-yet-peer-reviewed evidence from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease emergency offers some support for this concern: an analysis of public commentary on video-sharing platforms during the outbreak found that discourse was substantially shaped by institutional mistrust, misinformation and comparisons with unrelated past health emergencies, alongside expressions of trust (6). This is consistent with, but does not directly confirm, an expectation-related mistrust pathway of the kind this Perspective proposes.This Perspective proposes that East Africa’s experience with Ebola vaccine preparedness may be creating a new public health challenge, which we term the vaccination paradox: preparedness success may increase confidence, and confidence may in turn generate expectation. Where expectations exceed what vaccine science can immediately deliver, outbreak response could face avoidable mistrust although the existence and magnitude of this effect have not yet been measured. Based on a non-systematic review of the peer-reviewed and gray literature described below, we are not aware of prior work that conceptualizes this dynamic as a distinct preparedness risk in East or Central African Ebola control; we offer this as our reading of the literature rather than as a systematic bibliometric claim. We therefore introduce a hypothesis-generating framework linking vaccine science, community expectation, risk communication and regional outbreak governance, grounded explicitly in expectation-disconfirmation theory (7) and crisis and emergency risk communication theory (8).Distinguishing evidence, interpretation and hypothesisThroughout this Perspective we distinguish three categories of claim. First, established findings: facts documented in the cited primary literature, such as the existence of licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccines or the case counts of specific outbreaks. Second, interpretations: our reading of what those findings plausibly imply, stated explicitly as interpretation. Third, hypotheses: constructs and causal pathways that this Perspective proposes but that have not been directly tested, including the Vaccine Expectation Gap, Vaccine Anticipation, and the proposed pathway from vaccine success to expectation-related mistrust. analysis_zh.main_results: 我们建议审稿人、编辑和读者将这些假设视为研究议程,而不是已证明的准备风险。表1 疫苗期望差距框架用于东非埃博拉病毒准备。准备领域当前成就(已记录)新兴悖论(提出)战略回应(推荐)证据状态疫苗科学针对扎伊尔埃博拉病毒病的疫苗已获许可某些受众可能认为保护覆盖所有埃博拉病毒病促进针对特定物种的疫苗知识成就:已确立的发现。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 我们使用“埃博拉病毒病”特指由扎伊尔埃博拉病毒引起的疾病,使用“苏丹病毒病”和“邦迪布古病毒病”分别指由这两种病毒引起的疾病,而使用“埃博拉病毒病”或“埃博拉病”作为涵盖所有已知埃博拉病毒物种的广义术语,遵循世界卫生组织(WHO)当前的用法(3)。公众是否能够区分埃博拉病毒的不同物种,以及针对某一物种成功实施疫苗接种是否会产生对其他物种同样有效的预期,这些都是实证性问题,据我们所知,这些问题尚未在东非或中非地区直接进行研究。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 在实际应用中,领域可能会重叠,应根据当地的暴发历史、疫苗可用性和社区沟通需求进行调整。图1 修订后的疫苗在埃博拉病毒准备中的期望差距概念框架,区分了已记录的关系和提出的、假设的关系。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 我们建议,东非和中非地区埃博拉 疫苗 的下一步准备研究应实证检验,将更优的 疫苗 与有意的期望治理相结合是否能提高当任何一种埃博拉病毒物种再次出现时社区的信任度。

full_text: IntroductionHost-directed antiviral discovery requires a traceable route from host-factor identification to testable molecular hypotheses. This study developed such a workflow around a host factor associated with Ebola virus glycoprotein (EBOV GP).MethodsGFP-GP pulldown coupled with co-immunoprecipitation/mass spectrometry was used to identify GP-associated host candidates. A PSMD11/Rpn6-centred workflow integrated knowledge-graph inference, ligand-only machine learning, ADMETlab profiling and interface-guided docking. Candidate prioritization was assessed through score-weight sensitivity analysis, applicability-domain assessment and docking controls addressing seed reproducibility, search convergence, whole-receptor context and macrocycle ring-conformer sensitivity. Docking scores were contextualized against a matched 59-compound library.ResultsThe analysis recovered 424 GP-pulldown-specific host proteins and nominated PSMD11/Rpn6 as a proteostasis anchor. The tier-gated knowledge-graph candidate membership was invariant across the tested weight perturbations, with Spearman rho = 0.998 under equal weighting. The selected ExtraTrees model achieved an AUC of 0.912 for the Ki endpoint. Applicability-domain assessment and ADMET profiling differentiated candidate confidence and predicted liabilities. Docking reproducibility checks yielded a maximum standard deviation of 0.05 kcal/mol for conformationally restricted ligands, while macrocyclic candidates showed greater protocol-dependent variability. Rule-based triage integrating upstream evidence, ADMET burden, chemotype diversity and mechanistic coverage returned five candidates: betamethasone, bafilomycin A1, everolimus, pitavastatin and CHEMBL1410015.DiscussionThe workflow links a proteomic host-factor signal to a compact set of chemically diverse hypotheses with explicit evidence sources and limitations. The candidates remain hypotheses for experimental assessment; direct target engagement, interface blockade and antiviral activity are not established by the present study. 2Materials and methods2.1Co-IP/MS dataset and sample inclusionHEK293 Co-IP/MS data served as the experimental anchor. Two matched anti-GFP pulldown samples from the same batch were included: F005448, which expressed a GFP-GP fusion protein and served as the GFP-GP bait sample, and F005449, which expressed the pEGFP-C1 GFP empty vector and served as the GFP-only negative control. Both samples were subjected to anti-GFP bead enrichment, tryptic digestion and LC-MS/MS analysis. This paired design was intended to distinguish GFP-GP-associated complex signals from GFP- and bead-associated background within a shared tag and pulldown context. Samples were included when they originated from the same HEK293 Co-IP/MS experiment, had clearly defined bait or control constructs, contained traceable Mascot protein- and peptide-level outputs suitable for UniProt-accession-level merging, and had been searched with identical database parameters. Samples from unrelated expression conditions, samples lacking traceable Mascot outputs, or samples that did not directly support the GFP-GP versus GFP-only comparison were excluded.For orthogonal cell-level assessment of the GP-associated PSMD11/Rpn6 candidate, HeLa cells were co-transfected with GP-RFP and PSMD11-GFP or GFP-alone control. At 24–48 h after transfection, cells were washed twice with PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 15–20 min at room temperature, washed three times, permeabilized with 0.2%–0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10–15 min, and blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin or 10% normal goat serum for 1 h. Coverslips were mounted with ProLong Gold antifade medium containing DAPI. Images were acquired using a confocal laser-scanning microscope with 488-nm, 561-nm and 405-nm excitation for GFP, RFP and DAPI, respectively, using a 60x or 63x oil-immersion objective. Channels were acquired sequentially to minimize crosstalk. The analysis assessed spatial overlap of GP-RFP and PSMD11-GFP; it was not used to infer direct binding.2.2LC-MS/MS search, preprocessing and quality controlRaw LC-MS/MS data were searched with Mascot against SwissProt, using established database-search logic for probability-based protein identification and the curated UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot protein sequence resource (Perkins et al., 1999; The UniProt Consortium, 2017; Boutet et al., 2007). Search settings included trypsin specificity, a maximum of one missed cleavage, cysteine carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification, methionine oxidation as a variable modification, 10 ppm precursor mass tolerance, 0.6 Da fragment mass tolerance, monoisotopic mass values and a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Each sample contained 30,639 MS/MS queries. The use of identical database versions, digestion rules, modification settings and mass tolerances ensured that the two samples were compared within the same search space. Mascot protein-level reports were merged at the UniProt accession level. Proteins not detected in a sample were assigned values of 0 for Mascot score, unique peptide count and sequence coverage only for presence/absence classification; these values were not interpreted as true abundance estimates. Proteins were categorized as GP-pulldown-only preliminary candidates, shared/non-specific proteins, or control-specific proteins according to their detection pattern in F005448 and F005449. PSMD11/Rpn6 peptide-level evidence was extracted from Mascot peptide exports and protein reports and verified by exact matching to the canonical sequence (UniProt O00231). PSMD11/Rpn6 was considered eligible as a host anchor if it was detected in GFP-GP pulldown, absent from the matched GFP-only control and supported by peptide sequences matching the canonical PSMD11/Rpn6 sequence.2.3PSMD11/Rpn6-centred heterogeneous knowledge graphA PSMD11/Rpn6-centred heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph was constructed by integrating curated literature evidence, DRKG-derived compound-gene target edges, proteasome/proteostasis module annotations, viral host-interaction context, MS seed evidence and manually audited triples. Entity types included genes/proteins, compounds, pathways, diseases, viral contexts and literature-derived evidence nodes. Relation types included compound-target, host-machinery, proteasome-module, PSMD11/Rpn6-neighbourhood, shared-anchor transfer and embedding-supported completion candidates. Known PSMD11/Rpn6 probes, direct PSMD11/Rpn6 knowledge-graph evidence compounds and classical proteasome inhibitors were retained as audit or control references. The discovery queue was generated from inference-only candidates to avoid allowing known direct probes or canonical proteasome inhibitors to dominate exploratory ranking.2.4Knowledge-graph inference scoringCandidate ranking used a predefined heuristic triage score rather than a model trained on an external validation set: KG score=0.48×TransE_supported+0.20×PSMD11_neighbor+0.19×proteasome_module+0.13×shared_anchor_transfer−target_count_penalty TransE_supported denotes embedding-supported completion evidence; PSMD11_neighbor denotes proximity to the PSMD11/Rpn6 neighbourhood; proteasome_module denotes association with proteasome or proteostasis modules; shared_anchor_transfer denotes indirect inference through shared host or mechanistic anchors; and target_count_penalty reduces the discovery priority of broad-target candidates. The final KG top20 used a rule-tiered queue, with ranks 1–12 retaining candidates with contextual PSMD11-side evidence and ranks 13–20 serving as TransE-only reserve candidates. These weights were fixed before scoring, so the queue is reproducible from the published formula and candidate nomination is governed by the staged tier rules rather than by the raw score. To make the effect of this choice explicit, KG score-weight sensitivity was assessed under equal component weights, single-component perturbations (×0.5-×1.5), target-count-penalty perturbations and random Dirichlet weight perturbations (Supplementary Figure S1; Supplementary Table S6).2.5Ligand-only machine learning affinity filteringTraining data were derived from PDBbind protein-ligand binding records and split into IC50, Kd and Ki endpoint tables. The KG top20 candidates were subjected to ligand-only machine-learning filtering using canonical SMILES as input. Compounds that could not be parsed into valid molecular objects or feature matrices were excluded. Molecular features consisted of Morgan/ECFP4 2048-bit fingerprints and ten RDKit physicochemical descriptors: molecular weight, MolLogP, topological polar surface area, hydrogen-bond donor count, hydrogen-bond acceptor count, rotatable-bond count, aromatic-ring count, heteroatom count, fraction Csp3 and heavy-atom count (Rogers and Hahn, 2010; Landrum, 2013; Bento et al., 2020). Binary classification heads were trained separately for IC50, Kd and Ki endpoints using predefined train/test/validation splits. The IC50 dataset contained 4,301 samples (2,567 training, 868 test and 866 validation samples); the Kd dataset contained 6,466 samples (3,876 training, 1,298 test and 1,292 validation samples); and the Ki dataset contained 3,434 samples (2,054 training, 690 test and 690 validation samples). Extra Trees, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting and Linear SVM models were compared using AUC, AUPR, accuracy, F1 score, Matthews correlation coefficient and confusion matrices (Geurts et al., 2006; Breiman, 2001; Hosmer et al., 2013; Friedman, 2001; Jakkula, 2006; Rainio et al., 2024).A composite machine-learning score was defined as: ML score=0.70×Ki+0.20×IC50+0.10×Kd Ki was weighted most strongly because it is more directly related to binding or inhibition constants and because the Ki classifier showed the best internal performance in this analysis. IC50 was used as a functional-activity support signal and Kd as a reference signal. The ML score quantifies relative activity tendency within the available bioactivity feature space, which is the axis this layer is designed to contribute. The endpoint weights were likewise fixed before scoring, and endpoint-weight sensitivity was assessed under equal weights, single-endpoint perturbations and Dirichlet perturbations (Supplementary Figure S2; Supplementary Table S6). To define the chemical space in which each score is supported, the applicability domain of the ligand-only models was audited against the endpoint-specific training ligands using ECFP4 nearest-neighbour Tanimoto similarity together with RDKit descriptor-range checks, and each candidate was classified as inside or well supported, borderline or mixed, or extrapolative (Supplementary Figure S3; Supplementary Table S7).2.6ADMET risk stratificationML top12 candidates were profiled with ADMETLab 3.0, an online ADMET prediction platform for absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity assessment (Fu et al., 2024). Risk categories included hERG/QT liability, drug-induced liver injury, Ames/genotoxicity, organ toxicity, CYP-related drug-drug interaction, assay interference, physicochemical out-of-range properties, absorption and solubility. Because EBOV persists in immune-privileged central-nervous-system sites while acute replication is systemic, both predicted CNS access and predicted peripheral restriction are informative, so the endpoint was recorded for all candidates rather than applied as a pass/fail criterion (Supplementary Figure S4; Supplementary Table S7). A local overall_admet_risk_proxy was derived from ADMETLab outputs to summarize relative risk burden within this candidate set. This proxy supports within-cohort prioritization and is reported alongside the individual ADMETLab endpoints. The structural follow-up shortlist was then selected by explicit triage rules: candidates with broad ADMET red flags were shifted to comparator/control roles; the remaining candidates had to retain at least one upstream support signal from KG or ML; chemically or mechanistically redundant options were collapsed to one representative; and the final set was required to cover distinct, experimentally interpretable mechanisms while remaining compatible with interface docking. The final five candidates therefore constitute the structural follow-up shortlist produced by these staged rules, each entering with a named evidence source.2.7Interface definition and molecular dockingStructural follow-up focused on pockets near the predicted PSMD11/Rpn6 and EBOV GP interface, rather than on arbitrary sites in isolated proteins. PSMD11/Rpn6 (UniProt O00231) and EBOV GP (UniProt Q05320) were modelled as a protein complex using AlphaFold 3, which predicts biomolecular structures and interactions across protein, nucleic-acid and small-molecule contexts (Fu et al., 2024). All five AlphaFold 3 complex models returned ipTM 0.14–0.15, pTM 0.41 and fraction disordered 0.27–0.29, so the complex was used to define an interface-proximal search region and the resulting docking evidence was bounded by the four control experiments described below. The selected exploratory model was used to define GP-contacting residues on the PSMD11/Rpn6 side, and nearby pockets, grooves and shallow cavities were selected for docking-box placement. Preliminary docking was performed using AutoDock Vina (Trott and Olson, 2010). The search box was centred on the PSMD11/Rpn6-side interface pocket derived from the AlphaFold 3 complex model and expanded with padding to cover adjacent grooves and cavities near the predicted GP-contacting surface. The complete grid specification is now reported: box centre (−11.079, 5.480, −0.367) Å and box dimensions 40.14 × 25.64 × 43.68 Å (volume 44,952 Å3), with grid spacing 0.375 Å, exhaustiveness 8, energy_range 3 kcal/mol and num_modes 9; receptor and ligands were prepared as rigid-receptor PDBQT files and the per-run random seeds are listed in Supplementary Table S8. This box encloses 28.5% of receptor heavy atoms and 138 of 422 PSMD11/Rpn6 residues, defining a regional search volume around the predicted interface that covers the interface footprint together with its adjacent grooves and cavities. Docking poses were inspected in PyMOL to evaluate their spatial placement relative to the putative interface and to generate structural visualizations (DeLano, 2002).To define the boundary conditions of the docking evidence, four control experiments were performed on the archived receptor and ligand files. First, each reported pose was re-docked with the archived configuration under five random seeds, and again at exhaustiveness 32, to quantify reproducibility and search convergence. Second, a whole-receptor blind-docking control (108 × 68 × 84 Å box covering the entire PSMD11/Rpn6 model) was run under five seeds to test whether non-interface pockets yield equal or better predicted scores. Third, because Bafilomycin A1 and Everolimus are macrocycles, both were re-prepared with a macrocycle-aware protocol in which ring bonds are broken with glue pseudo-atoms so that ring conformation is sampled during docking, and were additionally docked as a 20-member ETKDGv3 ring-conformer ensemble; these were compared against the rigid-ring preparation used originally. Fourth, the KG-scored candidate pool (59 ligands comprising the PSMD11-side target-transfer and TransE-completion tiers, with the published audit anchors and proteasome-inhibitor positive controls removed) was docked into the identical interface box to establish the score distribution expected for an arbitrary compound of this class in this volume. All control runs used AutoDock Vina 1.2.5; scripts, logs and per-run outputs are provided in the revision package (Supplementary Figures S5-S7; Supplementary Tables S8-S11). 3ResultsThe initial GFP-GP pulldown signal was converted into an experimentally anchored candidate-discovery path (Figure 1). Co-IP/MS first tested whether the GP bait enriched a host-candidate space distinct from GFP-associated background. PSMD11/Rpn6 was then used as a proteostasis-related anchor to constrain knowledge graph inference, machine learning model, ADMET assessment and interface-focused docking.FIGURE 1PSMD11/Rpn6-centred workflow for prioritizing EBOV GP-associated proteostasis candidates.Infographic depicts a two-step framework for antiviral drug discovery targeting PSMD11. Step 1 shows experimental discovery with GFP-GP pulldown, mass spectrometry, and identification of PSMD11/Rpn6. Step 2 presents computational prioritization: (2.1) a knowledge graph layer identifies top candidates, (2.2) machine learning ranks candidates, (2.3) ADMET screening assesses risk, and (2.4) interface docking evaluates binding affinity, producing a prioritized drug set including betamethasone and everolimus.3.1Co-IP/MS identifies PSMD11/Rpn6 as a GP-pulldown-associated proteostasis anchorCo-IP/MS identified 1,286 distinct UniProt accessions across the GFP-GP pulldown and matched GFP-only control. The critical observation was selective rather than quantitative: PSMD11/Rpn6 fell within the GFP-GP-associated candidate space and was absent from the GFP-only background (Figure 2a). The overall classification of 424 GP-pulldown-only proteins, 641 shared proteins and 221 control-specific proteins defined the experimental background against which this signal was interpreted (Figure 2b). The PSMD11/Rpn6-specific evidence then localized the anchor within this background: the protein-level summary confirmed its detection pattern (Figure 2c), and peptide mapping placed the representative peptide EQSILELGSLLAK at residues 47–59 with a Mascot ion score of 33.9 (Figure 2d,e). PSMD11/Rpn6 was therefore advanced as a selectively detected proteasome subunit combining biological relevance to UPS/proteostasis and viral host-dependence contexts with prior chemical tractability established in PSMD11/Rpn6 small-molecule studies. Panel f contains confocal images for PSMD11-GFP and GFP-control conditions, with columns showing GP-RFP in red, GFP in green, DAPI in blue and merged channels. Scale bars indicate 10 micrometres.To provide orthogonal cellular context for this nomination, we examined the spatial distribution of GP-RFP and PSMD11-GFP by confocal imaging. GP-RFP and PSMD11-GFP showed prominent spatial overlap in cytoplasmic and perinuclear regions, whereas the GFP-alone control did not reproduce this concentrated overlap pattern (Figure 2f). This observation places the two proteins in shared intracellular compartments and adds an orthogonal cellular evidence layer to the proteomic nomination of PSMD11/Rpn6 as a GP-associated host candidate.3.2PSMD11/Rpn6-centred KG separates contextual candidates from TransE-only reservesThe knowledge-graph layer converted the PSMD11/Rpn6 pulldown signal into an interpretable candidate queue in which every nomination is traceable to a named evidence component. The graph projection placed PSMD11/Rpn6 within a heterogeneous biomedical neighbourhood spanning proteins, compounds, viral-context terms, pathways and literature-derived evidence nodes (Figure 3a). Relation and source summaries confirmed that this neighbourhood draws on multiple independent evidence classes, including proteostasis-relevant relations, viral host context, DRKG-derived edges, curated literature, the MS seed and manually audited triples (Figure 3b,c). Known PSMD11/Rpn6 probes, direct PSMD11/Rpn6 evidence compounds and classical proteasome inhibitors were held as audit references, which keeps the exploratory ranking from collapsing onto already-characterized chemistry.FIGURE 3Literature evidence and heterogeneous biomedical KG construction centred on PSMD11/Rpn6. The two-tier display separates context-supported candidates from reserve-only TransE hits, so contextual evidence governs nomination while reserve hits remain visible for later exploration (Figure 4c), and the evidence decomposition reports which component carried each candidate before ML and ADMET profiling (Figure 4d). The result is a KG top-20 queue delivered to ligand-only ML filtering (Supplementary Table S1), with each entry annotated by its supporting mechanism: CHEMBL1410015 led the queue on a USP14-linked transfer signal combined with low target_count, while Everolimus, Betamethasone and Pitavastatin entered as mTOR/proteostasis, steroid and metabolic-transfer hypotheses respectively. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionHost-directed antiviral discovery has produced extensive catalogues of virus-associated host factors, yet converting these catalogues into testable chemical hypotheses remains the rate-limiting step. Computational repurposing addresses the complementary problem, exploring chemical space rapidly while lacking experimentally derived biological anchors. The present work connects the two. GFP-GP pulldown Co-IP/MS identified PSMD11/Rpn6 as a GP-associated proteostasis component, and knowledge-graph inference, ligand-based machine learning, ADMET assessment and interface-oriented docking were then applied around that single anchor to generate a compact set of prioritized compounds.PSMD11/Rpn6 is a regulatory-particle subunit of the 26S proteasome that governs proteasome assembly and substrate-processing capacity. EBOV GP biosynthesis imposes a heavy load on host quality control through extensive folding, dense glycosylation and multi-compartment trafficking, so enrichment of a proteasome assembly factor in the GP pulldown relative to the matched GFP-only control links GP expression to proteostasis regulation. Co-IP/MS reports co-capture within a complex, which is consistent with direct binding, indirect recruitment, shared localization or a GP-induced shift in quality-control machinery. PSMD11/Rpn6 therefore functions here as a biologically motivated anchor for compound discovery. Among the 424 proteins detected only in the GP condition, it was selected on canonical peptide support, a defined role in the regulatory particle, published chemical tractability and the mechanistic link between proteostasis and viral glycoprotein maturation.The resulting candidates carry distinct evidence signatures rather than positions on a single scale. The knowledge graph supplies biological context around PSMD11/Rpn6, machine learning estimates activity tendency within known chemical-biological space, ADMET profiling addresses pharmacological feasibility, and docking supplies structural compatibility hypotheses. Betamethasone emerged as a steroid-associated representative combining favourable predicted activity with acceptable ADMET properties. Bafilomycin A1 entered as a pathway-oriented comparator through its established relationship with V-ATPase, lysosomal regulation and proteostasis. Everolimus and Pitavastatin represent mTOR-associated and metabolic-regulatory mechanisms. CHEMBL1410015 is a knowledge-graph-driven exploratory candidate supported by a USP14-linked inference signal and a low target-count penalty. Reading the output by mechanistic role preserves more biological information than a single composite score, since compounds entering through different evidence layers demand different validation experiments.Sensitivity analysis of the scoring framework supports this prioritization. Equal component weighting, single-component perturbation, variation of the target-count penalty and random Dirichlet weight sampling all reproduced consistent candidate rankings (Supplementary Figure S1; Supplementary Table S6). Candidate selection thus reflects the combined contribution of several evidence dimensions rather than one predefined weighting configuration.The scope of the present evidence is defined by three features of the study design. The Co-IP/MS analysis used one pulldown sample per condition, so the GP-associated signal establishes a candidate rather than a quantified interaction. Support for PSMD11/Rpn6 rests on proteomic enrichment and cellular localization, leaving direct molecular contact and interface geometry open. The HEK293 GFP-GP overexpression system offers a controlled discovery platform in which replication dynamics, endogenous GP levels and host responses differ from those of EBOV infection.Structural uncertainty likewise shapes what the computational analyses can claim. The predicted GP-PSMD11/Rpn6 complex carries low interface confidence, and blind docking distributed poses broadly across the receptor without favouring the predicted interface. Under these conditions, trajectory-based and physics-based rescoring methods characterize the behaviour of one selected model and report free energies for an arrangement that structural evidence does not yet single out. Their interpretive value depends on an experimentally supported binding site and a constrained pose, which cross-linking mass spectrometry, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, truncation analysis and site-directed mutagenesis are positioned to provide. We are therefore pursuing interface characterization as the step that makes molecular dynamics and MM-GBSA/MM-PBSA analysis mechanistically informative.Our validation programme follows the order in which this evidence must be established. We are first establishing the GP-PSMD11/Rpn6 association through reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation, endogenous-level detection and interface mapping. Direct compound engagement with PSMD11/Rpn6 will then be measured by orthogonal biophysical methods together with cellular target-engagement assays. Functional experiments, including competition assays, genetic perturbation and rescue, will test whether the candidates modulate GP-associated processes through PSMD11/Rpn6. Antiviral activity will be assessed in GP-pseudotyped entry systems and, where the biosafety context permits, authentic EBOV infection models, with pathway-matched counterscreens and cytotoxicity profiling to separate host-targeted mechanisms from the established pharmacological activities of the repurposed compounds.Taken together, these results identify PSMD11/Rpn6-associated proteostasis as a plausible and experimentally addressable entry point for EBOV GP-focused host-directed discovery. Integrating proteomic evidence, knowledge-guided inference, machine learning prioritization and structural analysis within one transparent framework offers a scalable route from host-factor signals to focused therapeutic hypotheses.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionThis study provides a host-anchored strategy for translating an EBOV GP-associated proteomics signal into prioritized, experimentally tractable small-molecule hypotheses. GFP-GP pulldown Co-IP/MS nominated PSMD11/Rpn6 as a GP-associated proteostasis candidate, and this anchor was used to organize knowledge-graph inference, ligand-only machine learning, ADMET risk stratification and interface-oriented docking into a coherent triage workflow. Betamethasone, Bafilomycin A1, Everolimus, Pitavastatin and CHEMBL1410015 constitute the rule-selected structural follow-up set, each carrying a defined level of network support, predicted activity tendency, risk burden and structural accommodation. This distinction is essential because host-directed antiviral discovery requires not only computational ranking but also explicit control of mechanism, toxicity and assay interpretability. The framework advances a reproducible path from AP-MS-derived host-candidate discovery to mechanism-aware molecular triage. It integrates a GP-associated experimental anchor, stable KG and ML candidate pools, ADMET-informed selection and a calibration-aware structural screen to deliver a chemically diverse, experiment-ready shortlist.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionEbola virus disease remains a major cause of high-fatality viral haemorrhagic fever, first recognized as a distinct filovirus disease in the 1970s and repeatedly associated with severe regional outbreaks thereafter (Feldmann and Geisbert, 2011). Although rVSV-vectored vaccination, monoclonal-antibody therapy and improved supportive care have strengthened outbreak responses, the clinical and public-health management of EBOV infection is still constrained by cryptic transmission, narrow treatment windows and the complexity of virus-host interactions (Henao-Restrepo et al., 2017; Mulangu et al., 2019). EBOV GP is the dominant viral envelope glycoprotein and mediates particle attachment, endocytosis, endosomal proteolytic priming, Niemann-Pick C1 (NPC1) engagement and membrane fusion (Kuroda et al., 2020; Bortz et al., 2020; Lane and Ekins, 2020; Plewe et al., 2020; Gaisina et al., 2020; Chandran et al., 2005; Carette et al., 2011; Kuroda et al., 2015; Gong et al., 2016; Simmons et al., 2016). It is therefore a central target of neutralizing antibodies, entry inhibitors and host-factor intervention strategies.Previous work has defined many of the core steps in GP-mediated entry. Proteolytic processing of GP within the endosomal-lysosomal pathway exposes receptor-binding determinants that allow NPC1 engagement and subsequent membrane fusion. NPC1 functions as a well-established intracellular receptor that links GP conformational priming to the fusion step of EBOV entry (Gong et al., 2016; Bornholdt et al., 2016; Ahmad et al., 2023). Its identification as an essential entry factor also provides a conceptual precedent for host-directed EBOV intervention, in which host proteins required for GP-mediated infection can be used as mechanistic anchors for antiviral discovery. Additional host factors, including TIM-1, the HOPS complex, PIKFYVE, GNPTAB, PIK3C3, SLC39A9 and glycosylation-related pathways have been supported by genetic screens, structural studies or infection models (Chandran et al., 2005; Carette et al., 2011; Kuroda et al., 2015; Gong et al., 2016; Simmons et al., 2016; Flint et al., 2019; Gong et al., 2024). Soluble GP, GP-induced endothelial signalling, GP conformational stability and GP glycosylation may also influence viral pathogenicity or entry efficiency (Bortz et al., 2020; Moni et al., 2022; Furuyama et al., 2021; Bagdonaite et al., 2024). Together, these findings indicate that GP-associated host dependence extends beyond a single receptor-binding event and involves endocytic trafficking, glycoprotein processing, membrane fusion, cellular stress responses and immune regulation.Compared with entry receptors and endocytic trafficking factors, GP-associated proteostasis nodes have been less systematically exploited for candidate molecule discovery. The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), endoplasmic-reticulum stress, the unfolded protein response and broader proteostasis machinery are recurrent host-dependence or host-restriction contexts during viral infection; proteostasis here refers to the integrated cellular network that maintains protein folding, trafficking, assembly and degradation capacity (Valerdi et al., 2021; Prasad and Greber, 2021; Balch et al., 2008). Viruses can reshape protein stability, replication-complex assembly, immune evasion and entry or egress through ubiquitination, deubiquitination, proteasomal degradation, folding burden and stress signal (Valerdi et al., 2021; Prasad and Greber, 2021; Lun et al., 2021; Umthong et al., 2021; Song et al., 2021; Abad et al., 2023). For enveloped viruses such as EBOV, the synthesis, glycosylation, folding and trafficking of large amounts of GP may itself impose a substantial burden on host quality-control systems. This provides a biological rationale for searching GP interactomes for proteostasis-associated host anchors.PSMD11/Rpn6 is a structural and regulatory subunit of the 19S regulatory particle lid of the 26S proteasome. Structural studies indicate that PSMD11/Rpn6 contributes to stabilization of the interface between the 19S regulatory particle and the 20S core particle, while changes in PSMD11/Rpn6 expression or function can alter proteasome activity and proteostasis output (Pathare et al., 2012; Lander et al., 2012). Small-molecule probe and target-fishing studies further suggest that PSMD11/Rpn6 is chemically interrogable (Tian and Trader, 2020; Dai et al., 2022). Moreover, PSMD11/Rpn6 loss-of-function has been linked to impaired 26S proteasome assembly and increased interferon-response phenotypes, placing PSMD11/Rpn6 at a possible intersection between proteostasis and immune regulation (Deb et al., 2024). These observations provide a plausible basis for evaluating it as a proteostasis anchor in a tiered discovery workflow.Host-directed antiviral discovery offers the potential advantage of targeting host dependencies that are not encoded by highly mutable viral genomes. However, this strategy faces two methodological difficulties. First, interactomics and genetic screens frequently generate large host-candidate lists, and without matched controls and explicit evidence stratification it is difficult to distinguish reproducible interactions from non-specific pulldown background, expression-burden effects or mechanistically relevant nodes. Second, host-targeted small molecules often carry liabilities related to broad targeting, cytotoxicity, immune modulation or pharmacokinetics; therefore, they should not be advanced on the basis of a single docking score, knowledge-graph rank or ligand-only machine-learning output. Knowledge graphs and graph-based drug-repurposing methods provide useful frameworks for integrating heterogeneous evidence (Zhu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023), but they require experimental anchoring to avoid becoming generic database-driven inference.We therefore adopted an experimental-anchor-first, computational-stratification-second strategy. Co-IP/MS was used to nominate GP-associated host signals; knowledge-graph inference was used to place candidates in a mechanistic network context; ligand-only machine learning was used to estimate relative bioactivity tendencies; ADMET profiling was used to constrain experimental risk; and interface docking was used to generate control-audited structural accommodation hypotheses. Using this framework, we asked whether PSMD11/Rpn6 can be nominated as a GP-pulldown-associated proteostasis candidate, whether PSMD11/Rpn6-centred computation can yield mechanistically interpretable and risk-stratified molecules, and which candidates are most suitable for testing GP-PSMD11/Rpn6 association, proteostasis-related phenotypes and compound perturbation effects. 2.1Co-IP/MS dataset and sample inclusionHEK293 Co-IP/MS data served as the experimental anchor. Two matched anti-GFP pulldown samples from the same batch were included: F005448, which expressed a GFP-GP fusion protein and served as the GFP-GP bait sample, and F005449, which expressed the pEGFP-C1 GFP empty vector and served as the GFP-only negative control. Both samples were subjected to anti-GFP bead enrichment, tryptic digestion and LC-MS/MS analysis. This paired design was intended to distinguish GFP-GP-associated complex signals from GFP- and bead-associated background within a shared tag and pulldown context. Samples were included when they originated from the same HEK293 Co-IP/MS experiment, had clearly defined bait or control constructs, contained traceable Mascot protein- and peptide-level outputs suitable for UniProt-accession-level merging, and had been searched with identical database parameters. Samples from unrelated expression conditions, samples lacking traceable Mascot outputs, or samples that did not directly support the GFP-GP versus GFP-only comparison were excluded.For orthogonal cell-level assessment of the GP-associated PSMD11/Rpn6 candidate, HeLa cells were co-transfected with GP-RFP and PSMD11-GFP or GFP-alone control. full_text_excerpt: This study developed such a workflow around a host factor associated with Ebola virus glycoprotein (EBOV GP).MethodsGFP-GP pulldown coupled with co-immunoprecipitation/mass spectrometry was used to identify GP-associated host candidates. The candidates remain hypotheses for experimental assessment; direct target engagement, interface blockade and antiviral activity are not established by the present study. IntroductionHost-directed antiviral discovery requires a traceable route from host-factor identification to testable molecular hypotheses. A PSMD11/Rpn6-centred workflow integrated knowledge-graph inference, ligand-only machine learning, ADMETlab profiling and interface-guided docking. Candidate prioritization was assessed through score-weight sensitivity analysis, applicability-domain assessment and docking controls addressing seed reproducibility, search convergence, whole-receptor context and macrocycle ring-conformer sensitivity. Docking scores were contextualized against a matched 59-compound library.ResultsThe analysis recovered 424 GP-pulldown-specific host proteins and nominated PSMD11/Rpn6 as a proteostasis anchor. The tier-gated knowledge-graph candidate membership was invariant across the tested weight perturbations, with Spearman rho = 0.998 under equal weighting. The selected ExtraTrees model achieved an AUC of 0.912 for the Ki endpoint. Applicability-domain assessment and ADMET profiling differentiated candidate confidence and predicted liabilities. Docking reproducibility checks yielded a maximum standard deviation of 0.05 kcal/mol for conformationally restricted ligands, while macrocyclic candidates showed greater protocol-dependent variability. full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02506-0 Comment Acute infection as a driver of chronic diseases and the unsung benefits of vaccination In Su Cheon, Mark T. Esser & Jie Sun Acute infections can leave durable biological imprints that alter host physiology, chronic disease susceptibility, long-term health and even biological ageing, well after pathogen clearance. Vaccines should therefore be evaluated not only on their ability to prevent acute illness, but also on their efficacy in preventing or mitigating these long-lasting biological imprints and infection-associated chronic conditions. From microbial exposure and symptom onset to clinical recovery, acute infection has traditionally been viewed as a temporary distur- bance of host physiology. This view has shaped clinical care, public health policy and vaccine evaluation. However, growing clinical and experimental evidence indicates that this view is increasingly outdated. Many pathogens can cause symptoms that persist well beyond clear- ance of the infectious agent. Long COVID, also known as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection, is the best example and has raised public awareness of infection-associated chronic conditions and ill- nesses (IACCIs)1. It is estimated that at least 400 million individuals worldwide currently suffer from long COVID. The broad definition of long COVID describes a post-acute condition in which symptoms usually occur or persist 3 months after infection onset, last for at least 2 months, and cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis2. Com- mon symptoms include chronic fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog or exercise-intolerance. Long COVID demonstrates that, even after the acute phase has been resolved, infection can leave a persistent host state that impairs long-term quality of life. IACCI occurrence is not unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection and has been reported after other acute respiratory viral infections3. Systemic or local- ized infections have been associated with chronic illnesses that can last months to years, including group A Streptococcus, Lyme disease, influenza virus, Ebola virus, dengue and Epstein–Barr virus4. The lingering ‘tails’ of infectious disease can be generally understood as a failure to return fully to baseline after the initial illness. IACCIs often share a core series of common symptoms, including chronic fatigue, cognitive problems, sleep disorders and pain, while also displaying pathogen-specific heterogene- ity. Together, these syndromes establish an essential principle: the end of acute infection is not necessarily the end of the disease. More broadly, infections differ substantially in their long-term host legacy (see Box 1). Impacts on pre-existing chronic disease and the development of new chronic illness Acute infection can also alter the trajectory of chronic disease. By induc- ing injury, inflammation, tissue remodelling and systemic stress, acute infection can exacerbate or accelerate pre-existing chronic diseases and, in some settings, contribute to the initiation of new chronic ill- ness. For example, acute respiratory infections commonly exacerbate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Acute idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis exacerbations by infec- tions not only increase acute morbidity and mortality but can accel- erate the progression of fibrotic lung conditions and leave survivors with persistent loss of lung function. In this context, acute infection is not simply an added complication, but causes a stepwise injury and tissue remodelling that shifts patients onto a worse disease trajectory5. An even more provocative possibility is that acute infections can contribute to the development of new chronic diseases, including cancer. Large cohort studies have shown increased post-acute risks of chronic conditions including new onset of diabetes and autoimmun- ity development after SARS-CoV-2 infection6. Furthermore, elevated cardiovascular risk can persist for months, not only after infection with SARS-CoV-2, but also after influenza or respiratory syncytial virus infection, increasing in a graded fashion with acute disease severity6,7. Persistent or latent infections, such as human papillomavirus and hepatitis viruses, are well-established drivers of cancer development. However, emerging evidence suggests that even acute, non-persistent infections can influence cancer biology by reshaping tissue micro- environments after pathogen clearance. For instance, prior severe respiratory viral infection with SARS-CoV-2 or influenza was linked to accelerated lung cancer growth in mouse models and increased subsequent lung cancer risk among patients hospitalized for COVID-19 (ref. 8). In this context, severe viral injury potentially leaves behind a durable tissue, immune and epigenetic ‘scar’ that alters the local microenvironment, modifies future cancer risk and promotes tumour development under permissive conditions. Together, these observations support a model in which acute infection should be considered not only as an exacerbator of underly- ing chronic diseases, but as a potential cause of chronic diseases. This reframes the central clinical inquiry from a narrow focus on immedi- ate outcomes to a broader analysis of long-term consequences after acute infection. Addressing the latter question will require long-term clinical follow-up that extends well beyond the apparent acute recov- ery. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how transient infectious events fundamentally and persistently rewire host epigenetic, molecular and cellular pathways across the body. Such clinical and scientific efforts will be essential for understanding how acute infections leave durable host imprints and for developing interventions that protect against not only acute illness, but also its long-term consequences. Acute infection can accelerate biological ageing Ageing is the most important risk factor for the development of many chronic diseases, including heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s dis- ease. Increasing evidence suggests that acute infections can accelerate Check for updates nature microbiology Comment features of biological ageing. Studies using DNA methylation-based epi- genetic clocks have revealed accelerated epigenetic age in patients with COVID-19, particularly in those with severe disease9. Beyond the acute phase, post-COVID-19 cohorts show persistent altered immune ageing10, suggesting that infection can leave a durable imprint in pro-ageing path- ways. Together, these studies support a model in which SARS-CoV-2 infection can shift the host towards an older biological state. Similar observations are emerging from other acute infections. Influenza virus infection can promote cellular senescence in the lung, and the depletion of senescent cells reduces persistent lung pathology and improves epithelial repair in mouse models11. These findings support a model in which acute infection can function as a stressor to enhance tissue senescence and ageing, which in turn drives post-infection tissue remodelling. Although definitive evidence is still currently lacking, acute infection may shift the host towards a state of premature biological ageing and shortened health span or even life span, by possibly engaging multiple hallmarks of ageing, including chronic inflammation, DNA damage, telomere attrition, epigenetic remodelling, cellular senescence and so on. Nevertheless, this may help explain why a single infectious insult can produce persistent, systemic or multi-organ chronic consequences long after pathogen clearance. Vaccine efficacy beyond acute infection If acute infections can cause post-acute syndromes, worsen chronic dis- ease, initiate new chronic illness and accelerate biological ageing, then anti-microbial agents and vaccines must confer benefits that extend far beyond the prevention of immediate illness. Yet most vaccine efficacy and effectiveness trials measure only short-term endpoints including infection, disease mitigation, and prevention of acute hospitalization and death. These outcomes are important but capture only the acute phase of host protection. Observational studies and meta-analyses indicate that vacci- nation before SARS-CoV-2 infection reduces the risk of long COVID. Notably, a nationwide French cohort of 28 million adults found that mRNA COVID-19-vaccinated individuals had lower all-cause mortal- ity over 4 years, strongly suggesting that COVID-19 vaccination ben- efited long-term health outcomes12. Similarly, the influenza vaccine is another well-documented example of an immunization that prevents the onset and exacerbation of deleterious chronic conditions, includ- ing cardiovascular events13. These findings highlight a limitation of most vaccine studies. A vaccine that does not fully provide sterilizing immunity (such as cur- rent COVID-19 vaccines or influenza vaccines) may still reduce viral burden, inflammatory amplification, organ damage and downstream chronic disease risk. Thus, the long-term benefit of vaccination may be substantial even when acute protection against infection appears incomplete or modest, as long as it ameliorates disease severity during the acute phase. In this sense, vaccines should be viewed not only as tools to prevent acute infectious disease, but also as disease-modifying interventions that may preserve long-term organ function, immune homeostasis, health span and survival. In a climate of vaccine fatigue and declining public trust, a more complete accounting of vaccine benefits is both scientifically necessary and socially urgent. The public are often told that vaccines prevent infection or acute illness. That is true, but incomplete. The underappreciated benefit of vaccination may be protection of the future health of the individual, particularly by reducing the lifetime burden of diseases that can be initiated or accelerated by an acute infection. BOX 1 The long-term host legacies of infection Infections may differ in their capacity to leave a durable imprint on host health. Recognizing which infections commonly carry a long-lasting host legacy, and those for which such effects have not been consistently demonstrated, could help identify where infection prevention may provide long-term benefits. Infections that leave a harmful legacy Examples of infections that lead to chronic sequelae, exacerbate pre-existing diseases, cause new chronic conditions or accelerate biological ageing4: SARS-CoV-2 (long COVID, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and accelerated ageing); influenza (long flu and cardiovascular conditions); respiratory syncytial virus (asthma risk and cardiovascular events); Epstein–Barr virus (multiple sclerosis and cancer); group A Streptococcus (rheumatic heart disease and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis); poliovirus (post-polio syndrome); measles (immune amnesia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis); Mycobacterium tuberculosis (post-tuberculosis lung disease); Borrelia burgdorferi (post-treatment Lyme syndrome); and Ebola (post-Ebola syndrome). No consistently established long-term legacy For some generally self-limited infections such as common cold coronavirus and adenovirus infections, durable population-level sequelae have not been systematically demonstrated. This category may reflect limited long-term follow-up rather than proof that such infections are harmless in the long run. Microbial exposures associated with potentially beneficial immune calibration Early life exposure to commensal microbiota and diverse environmental microorganisms may help to calibrate immune development15. The hygiene hypothesis proposes that reduced exposure to microorganisms with which humans co-evolved may contribute to increased allergic and autoimmune risk later in life. Certain helminth and microbial pathogen exposures (such as hookworm and Helicobacter pylori) have also been associated with immuno­ regulatory effects. Nevertheless, these organisms can themselves cause substantial morbidity and should not be considered as inherently beneficial. Live attenuated vaccines such as Bacillus Calmette–Guérin can induce trained innate immune responses and may provide heterologous protection in some settings without the pathological legacy of natural infection. nature microbiology Comment We therefore propose a two-axis framework for vaccine evaluation in the future (Fig. 1). The first axis measures acute protection, that is, what has already been implemented, such as infection rate, sympto- matic diseases, hospitalization and death. The second axis, which we view as important, measures chronic protection, including the preven- tion or attenuation of IACCIs, pre-existing condition exacerbation, new-onset chronic disease, accelerated biological ageing, health span loss and/or long-term mortality. Different vaccines may perform differ- ently across these parameters. Some may strongly prevent infection, while others may primarily reduce chronic sequelae of acute infection. We think that the protection of both acute and chronic illness matters and should be clearly communicated to the public. To implement this broader framework, vaccine trials and real-world effectiveness studies should include longer follow-up and, where possible, connect study participants to electronic health records and chronic disease registries so that later outcomes can be measured systematically. Such long-term tracking would not only clarify the full impact of vaccination on host health but also provide rigorous evidence to counter misinformation that vaccines cause long-term harm. These studies should also use standardized definitions for IACCIs and track outcomes that reflect long-term health, including new or worsening chronic diseases, and measures of biological ageing, frailty, functional decline and extended all-cause mortality. A practical limitation to this recommendation is cost. Imple- menting such studies could cost hundreds of millions of dollars if performed as a randomized controlled clinical trial. Registry-enabled pragmatic, randomized trials offer one approach to improve feasibility. For example, the DANFLU-2 trial randomized aged adults to high-dose or standard-dose inactivated influenza vaccine and used routinely collected health-registry data for outcome ascertainment. In the pre- specified FLUNITY-HD pooled analysis of DANFLU-2, high-dose vaccina- tion was associated with fewer hospitalizations for heart failure than standard-dose vaccination in an exploratory outcome analysis14. Public health and cost-effectiveness models should similarly include chronic disease burden when estimating the value of vaccination. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how prior vaccination prevents or reduces the pathogen-driven and host inflammatory path- ways that lead to chronic disease, impaired tissue repair, accelerated biological ageing or decreased health and life span. Conclusion Acute infection should no longer be treated as a short-lived episode with only temporary consequences. It can be an origin point for long-term chronic disease, a modifier of chronic illness and a possible accelerator of biological ageing. Recognizing this chronic host legacy will reshape infection biology, chronic disease research and vaccine evaluation. The true burden of infection is therefore not limited to acute morbid- ity and mortality, but extends to the occurrence of chronic diseases, functional decline and biological ageing trajectories that may emerge months or years later. Likewise, the true value of vaccination should not be measured only by whether it prevents acute illness today, but also by whether it protects the future health of the individual.
