full_text_sections.full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02506-0 Comment Acute infection as a driver of chronic diseases and the unsung benefits of vaccination In Su Cheon, Mark T. Esser & Jie Sun Acute infections can leave durable biological imprints that alter host physiology, chronic disease susceptibility, long-term health and even biological ageing, well after pathogen clearance. Vaccines should therefore be evaluated not only on their ability to prevent acute illness, but also on their efficacy in preventing or mitigating these long-lasting biological imprints and infection-associated chronic conditions. From microbial exposure and symptom onset to clinical recovery, acute infection has traditionally been viewed as a temporary distur- bance of host physiology. This view has shaped clinical care, public health policy and vaccine evaluation. However, growing clinical and experimental evidence indicates that this view is increasingly outdated. Many pathogens can cause symptoms that persist well beyond clear- ance of the infectious agent. Long COVID, also known as post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection, is the best example and has raised public awareness of infection-associated chronic conditions and ill- nesses (IACCIs)1. It is estimated that at least 400 million individuals worldwide currently suffer from long COVID. The broad definition of long COVID describes a post-acute condition in which symptoms usually occur or persist 3 months after infection onset, last for at least 2 months, and cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis2. Com- mon symptoms include chronic fatigue, shortness of breath, brain fog or exercise-intolerance. Long COVID demonstrates that, even after the acute phase has been resolved, infection can leave a persistent host state that impairs long-term quality of life. IACCI occurrence is not unique to SARS-CoV-2 infection and has been reported after other acute respiratory viral infections3. Systemic or local- ized infections have been associated with chronic illnesses that can last months to years, including group A Streptococcus, Lyme disease, influenza virus, Ebola virus, dengue and Epstein–Barr virus4. The lingering ‘tails’ of infectious disease can be generally understood as a failure to return fully to baseline after the initial illness. IACCIs often share a core series of common symptoms, including chronic fatigue, cognitive problems, sleep disorders and pain, while also displaying pathogen-specific heterogene- ity. Together, these syndromes establish an essential principle: the end of acute infection is not necessarily the end of the disease. More broadly, infections differ substantially in their long-term host legacy (see Box 1). Impacts on pre-existing chronic disease and the development of new chronic illness Acute infection can also alter the trajectory of chronic disease. By induc- ing injury, inflammation, tissue remodelling and systemic stress, acute infection can exacerbate or accelerate pre-existing chronic diseases and, in some settings, contribute to the initiation of new chronic ill- ness. For example, acute respiratory infections commonly exacerbate chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Acute idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis exacerbations by infec- tions not only increase acute morbidity and mortality but can accel- erate the progression of fibrotic lung conditions and leave survivors with persistent loss of lung function. In this context, acute infection is not simply an added complication, but causes a stepwise injury and tissue remodelling that shifts patients onto a worse disease trajectory5. An even more provocative possibility is that acute infections can contribute to the development of new chronic diseases, including cancer. Large cohort studies have shown increased post-acute risks of chronic conditions including new onset of diabetes and autoimmun- ity development after SARS-CoV-2 infection6. Furthermore, elevated cardiovascular risk can persist for months, not only after infection with SARS-CoV-2, but also after influenza or respiratory syncytial virus infection, increasing in a graded fashion with acute disease severity6,7. Persistent or latent infections, such as human papillomavirus and hepatitis viruses, are well-established drivers of cancer development. However, emerging evidence suggests that even acute, non-persistent infections can influence cancer biology by reshaping tissue micro- environments after pathogen clearance. For instance, prior severe respiratory viral infection with SARS-CoV-2 or influenza was linked to accelerated lung cancer growth in mouse models and increased subsequent lung cancer risk among patients hospitalized for COVID-19 (ref. 8). In this context, severe viral injury potentially leaves behind a durable tissue, immune and epigenetic ‘scar’ that alters the local microenvironment, modifies future cancer risk and promotes tumour development under permissive conditions. Together, these observations support a model in which acute infection should be considered not only as an exacerbator of underly- ing chronic diseases, but as a potential cause of chronic diseases. This reframes the central clinical inquiry from a narrow focus on immedi- ate outcomes to a broader analysis of long-term consequences after acute infection. Addressing the latter question will require long-term clinical follow-up that extends well beyond the apparent acute recov- ery. In parallel, mechanistic studies are needed to determine how transient infectious events fundamentally and persistently rewire host epigenetic, molecular and cellular pathways across the body. Such clinical and scientific efforts will be essential for understanding how acute infections leave durable host imprints and for developing interventions that protect against not only acute illness, but also its long-term consequences. Acute infection can accelerate biological ageing Ageing is the most important risk factor for the development of many chronic diseases, including heart disease, cancer and Alzheimer’s dis- ease. Increasing evidence suggests that acute infections can accelerate Check for updates nature microbiology Comment features of biological ageing. Studies using DNA methylation-based epi- genetic clocks have revealed accelerated epigenetic age in patients with COVID-19, particularly in those with severe disease9. Beyond the acute phase, post-COVID-19 cohorts show persistent altered immune ageing10, suggesting that infection can leave a durable imprint in pro-ageing path- ways. Together, these studies support a model in which SARS-CoV-2 infection can shift the host towards an older biological state. Similar observations are emerging from other acute infections. Influenza virus infection can promote cellular senescence in the lung, and the depletion of senescent cells reduces persistent lung pathology and improves epithelial repair in mouse models11. These findings support a model in which acute infection can function as a stressor to enhance tissue senescence and ageing, which in turn drives post-infection tissue remodelling. Although definitive evidence is still currently lacking, acute infection may shift the host towards a state of premature biological ageing and shortened health span or even life span, by possibly engaging multiple hallmarks of ageing, including chronic inflammation, DNA damage, telomere attrition, epigenetic remodelling, cellular senescence and so on. Nevertheless, this may help explain why a single infectious insult can produce persistent, systemic or multi-organ chronic consequences long after pathogen clearance. Vaccine efficacy beyond acute infection If acute infections can cause post-acute syndromes, worsen chronic dis- ease, initiate new chronic illness and accelerate biological ageing, then anti-microbial agents and vaccines must confer benefits that extend far beyond the prevention of immediate illness.
